events.text: Enfield calls the door place Black Mail House and muses.
events.quote: Black Mail House is what I call the place with the door

events.text: Utterson asks if the cheque drawer lives there.
events.quote: And you don’t know if the drawer of the cheque lives there?

events.text: Enfield says he noticed the drawer's address in some square.
events.quote: he lives in some square or other

events.text: Enfield explains his rule of not asking questions.
events.quote: I make it a rule of mine: the more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask

events.text: Enfield describes the door house: no other door, clean shut windows, smoking chimney.
events.quote: There is no other door, and nobody goes in or out of that one

events.text: Utterson asks the name of the man who walked over the child.
events.quote: I want to ask the name of that man who walked over the child

events.text: Enfield names the man as Hyde.
events.quote: It was a man of the name of Hyde

events.text: Enfield describes Hyde as deformed and detestable.
events.quote: He must be deformed somewhere; he gives a strong feeling of deformity

events.text: Utterson asks if Hyde used a key.
events.quote: You are sure he used a key?

events.text: Utterson says he already knows the other party's name.
events.quote: if I do not ask you the name of the other party, it is because I know it already

events.text: Enfield confirms Hyde still has the key and used it a week ago.
events.quote: The fellow had a key; and what’s more, he has it still

events.text: Enfield and Utterson agree never to refer to the matter again.
events.quote: Let us make a bargain never to refer to this again

relation_context.story_before_this_passage: 最近事件：Utterson and Enfield take their Sunday walk down a by-street.；Enfield points his cane at a sinister door and asks Utterson if he ever remarked it.；Enfield says the door is connected with a very odd story.；The man tramples over the girl's body and leaves her screaming.；Enfield collars the man and brings him back to the group around the child.；The doctor turns sick and white with desire to kill the prisoner.；They threaten scandal and force the man to pay a hundred pounds.；The man leads them to the door, unlocks it, and returns with gold and a cheque.；The man offers to stay until the banks open and cash the cheque himself.；They spend the night in Enfield's chambers and go to the bank next day.；Enfield presents the cheque believing it a forgery, but it proves genuine.
relation_context.previous_passage_tail:
make capital out of this accident,’ said he, ‘I am naturally helpless. No gentleman but wishes to avoid a scene,’ says he. ‘Name your figure.’ Well, we screwed him up to a hundred pounds for the child’s family; he would have clearly liked to stick out; but there was something about the lot of us that meant mischief, and at last he struck. The next thing was to get the money; and where do you think he carried us but to that place with the door?—whipped out a key, went in, and presently came back with the matter of ten pounds in gold and a cheque for the balance on Coutts’s, drawn payable to bearer and signed with a name that I can’t mention, though it’s one of the points of my story, but it was a name at least very well known and often printed. The figure was stiff; but the signature was good for more than that if it was only genuine. I took the liberty of pointing out to my gentleman that the whole business looked apocryphal, and that a man does not, in real life, walk into a cellar door at four in the morning and come out with another man’s cheque for close upon a hundred pounds. But he was quite easy and sneering. ‘Set your mind at rest,’ says he, ‘I will stay with you till the banks open and cash the cheque myself.’ So we all set off, the doctor, and the child’s father, and our friend and myself, and passed the rest of the night in my chambers; and next day, when we had breakfasted, went in a body to the bank. I gave in the cheque myself, and said I had every reason to believe it was a forgery. Not a bit of it. The cheque was genuine.”
[P10] “Tut-tut!” said Mr. Utterson.
